newsitem.title: Yugoslavia: Tension rises after Serbian opposition wins poll.
newsitem.headline: Tension rises after Serbian opposition wins poll.

text.p: Serbia's opposition urged its supporters on Wednesday to defend their sweeping victory in local elections and accused authorities of trying to reverse the results through massive fraud.
Opposition leaders said tensions were mounting in several major towns where local authorities had failed to verify voting results by Tuesday evening as required by law.

"In practically all towns in Serbia where we have won results are being cancelled, exactly to the extent it is necessary to cancel our victory and to give it to those who have lost the elections," Zoran Djindjic, head of the opposition Democratic Party, told reporters.
Authorities on Tuesday confirmed the opposition's victory in the capital Belgrade, a stunning blow to ruling Socialists led by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
But no results had been announced in several towns where the opposition said it scored clear majorities against the Socialists.
Djindjic and other leaders of the Zajedno (Together) called on their councillors across the country to uphold their legal rights and form new local governments.
"You should enter immediately into municipal and city assemblies, establish new authorities and defend them together with us," said a statement issued by the opposition.
Electoral commissions by law were required to confirm official results by Tuesday evening, 48 hours after polling stations closed.

"Such an illegal situation and attempt to reverse the will of the people is leading to a destabilisation of the state and the consequences could be very dramatic," Vesna Pesic, head of the opposition Civic Alliance, said.
The coalition later warned that Socialist authorities may be preparing to declare a state of emergency.
"The clear intention of the Socialist Party of Serbia to annul the election results is an introduction to a state of emergency in Serbia," an opposition statement said.
Opposition leaders said they would soon inform supporters about the timing of a "major" protest planned for the capital Belgrade.
Zajedno leaders said they planned to meet the Serbian justice minister to propose setting up a special independent commission to investigate fraud and resolve the crisis.

In the southern town of Nis, the local electoral commission announced on Wednesday that the ruling Socialists had an additional 11 seats in the city assembly due to unspecified irregularities, the Tanjug state news agency reported.
The opposition says it won a majority of 41 out of 70 seats in the Nis assembly.
A throng of some 30,000 protested in Nis on Tuesday night and special riot police were sent in to guard the city hall.
Zajedno leaders showed election documents to diplomats from the United States and European Union countries which they said proved their victory was legitimate.
Opposition coalition officials said privately they received no pledges from Western powers to pressurise Milosevic's government over the election results.
Diplomats view Milosevic as an important guarantor of stability in the region after he signed a peace agreement ending four years of war in Bosnia and Croatia.
"We know we have to fight our own battles," said one opposition official.
